extracted.intended_audience: educators, students, and the general public interested in news literacy
extracted.subtask_description: A pedagogical rubric for evaluating whether a piece of content is quality journalism (vs. opinion, propaganda, or low-quality reporting). Intended to guide educators and learners in identifying reliable news characteristics and red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Verified facts; correction policies; distinction between confirmed and reported
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report facts that have been checked; use correction policies when mistakes occur; clearly distinguish between confirmed information and unconfirmed or reported claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence
rubrics_metrics.description: Free of conflicts of interest; not beholden to sources, advertisers, or government
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relationships or dependencies that could influence coverage. Disclose relevant relationships when necessary and maintain editorial autonomy from advertisers, sources, and political actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple perspectives represented; no pre-judgment
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek and present diverse viewpoints, avoid assuming guilt or innocence before evidence, and strive for evenhanded coverage unless clearly labeled as opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect for sources and subjects; minimize harm
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat people with dignity, avoid unnecessary harm in reporting (particularly with vulnerable subjects), and consider ethical consequences of publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge mistakes; explain choices; engage criticism
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Own and correct errors publicly, explain editorial decisions when appropriate, and welcome or respond to reasonable criticism from the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose methods, sources where possible, funding
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open about how reporting was done, what sources were used (or why anonymity was granted), and who funds the reporting or organization when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: First-hand work, not aggregation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on primary reporting, on-the-ground observation, interviews, and original document review rather than merely rehashing others' work; clearly label aggregated or summarized content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing news from opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics that separate news and opinion (table of contrasts)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the table as a checklist: News aims to inform, presents multiple perspectives, minimizes bias, focuses on verifiable facts, quotes named sources, and answers 'what/how/why.' Opinion aims to argue, presents the author's view, has an explicit POV, includes interpretation, selectively quotes for argument, and uses 'should/why we should' framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple credible sources
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite several independent and relevant sources rather than relying on a single voice; include sources with differing perspectives when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific details
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete, specific information (e.g., 'Biggest flood since 1914' rather than 'biggest in recent memory')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer precise facts, dates, figures, and named examples over vague, relative, or anecdotal language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five W's + H answered
rubrics_metrics.description: Who, What, When, Where, Why, and How addressed, especially why it matters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quality piece should make clear the key facts and implications; answering 'why it matters' is emphasized as particularly important for newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straightforward language
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, direct wording (avoid sensational adjectives)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid loaded words like 'shocking' or 'unbelievable' and favor plain language that states facts without emotional manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-opinion separation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear demarcation between verified facts and interpretation or opinion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label analysis or opinion clearly and do not present interpretation as fact; separate the two within the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedge words noted
rubrics_metrics.description: Flagging uncertainty words such as 'think,' 'likely,' 'probably'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sources or evidence are uncertain, use hedging language and make that uncertainty explicit rather than overstating confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead has core information
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead contains core facts without bias
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening should summarize the essential facts (who/what/when/where/how/why) neutrally and avoid framing that implies an outcome or judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor's labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear labeling of opinion and other non-news formats
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark opinion pieces, sponsored content, or other formats clearly so readers know the nature and intent of the content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensational headline (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines that sensationalize content
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of headlines that use hyperbole or clickbait tactics; they often indicate low-quality or misleading reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single anonymous source on a major claim (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on one anonymous source for a major assertion
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Major claims should be corroborated by multiple sources or documented evidence; excessive reliance on a single anonymous source weakens credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: No links/citations to sources (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of links or citations supporting claims
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliable reporting should provide sources or links to documents, data, or statements that back key claims so readers can verify information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heavy adjectives (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of loaded descriptive language
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive adjective use signals bias or an attempt to persuade emotionally rather than inform; prefer neutral descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unanswerable claims (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that cannot be verified or tested
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of claims that lack a way to be checked or that rest on vague, unverifiable premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Click-bait formatting (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formatting designed to attract clicks rather than inform
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for listicles, sensational framing, or other layout choices prioritizing virality over substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Shocking’ or ‘you won't believe’ language (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases intended to provoke emotional surprise rather than convey fact
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such framing is typical of low-quality or deceptive content; prefer sober presentation of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-caps headlines (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines in all capital letters
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All-caps headlines are an attention-grabbing tactic often associated with low credibility or sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: No date or author byline (red flag)
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing basic metadata such as publication date or author
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credible journalism includes who wrote the piece and when; absence makes it harder to assess timeliness and accountability.
